kam1: What causes a hunched back, does it cause pain, and can exercise change the curve? Types of kyphosis, what studies found, the question of posture braces and six exercises to straighten the upper back at home.
kam3: Kyphosis is a noticeable forward rounding of the upper back, often called a hunched back. The most common type is postural kyphosis, which mostly affects teenagers. A mild curve often needs no treatment. Exercise can reduce the curve by a few degrees; the bigger gain is a stronger back and a more comfortable body.

kam17: Postural kyphosis: The most common type, mostly in teenagers and linked to poor posture.
kam18: Scheuermann’s kyphosis: The back of the spinal bones grows faster than the front, giving them a wedge shape.
kam19: Congenital kyphosis: The spine does not develop properly before birth; this is rare.
kam20: Spinal injury, arthritis and osteoporosis can also lead to a hunched back.
kam21: Is a hunched back the cause of pain?
kam22: A review of 54 studies found no strong link between the side-view curves of the spine and health problems, including back pain. So the advice to “sit up straight” does not explain pain on its own. Even so, staying in the same position for a long time can cause stiffness.
kam24: In 99 people over 60, back-strengthening exercise and posture training with a physiotherapist 3 days a week for 6 months reduced the kyphosis angle by 3 degrees compared with a control group and improved how people felt about their appearance; however, there was no difference in physical performance tests.
kam25: In studies of teenagers, 6–12 week corrective exercise and Pilates programmes reported reductions of between 2 and 9 degrees; the studies were small and long-term results are unknown.
kam27: Exercises that strengthen the back and trunk muscles support posture. If you have not exercised for a long time, you can check with a health professional first.
kam29: At a desk or when using your phone, you can try not to stay in the same position for long, and get up and stretch often.
kam31: Movements that open the chest and draw the shoulder blades back can bring relief to rounded shoulders.
kam32: If you are in pain, you can use paracetamol or an anti-inflammatory medicine after checking with your doctor or pharmacist.

kam35: In studies of teenagers, the pattern that seemed most effective was 2–3 days a week, 15–45 minutes, for 8–12 weeks. Do the movements slowly and with control, within a pain-free range.
kam36: Can a hunched back be corrected?
kam37: Postural kyphosis is flexible; the back can straighten when the person tries to stand tall. Reductions of a few degrees in the curve have been reported with exercise. The NHS, however, says physiotherapy can improve posture and ease pain and stiffness, but will not correct a structural curve.
kam38: Should I use a posture brace?
kam39: The NHS does not recommend a brace for postural kyphosis. A brace is only used in children with mild to moderate Scheuermann’s kyphosis, under specialist supervision. For posture, you can choose to strengthen your back muscles and change position often during the day.
kam40: Does a hunched posture cause back pain?
kam41: A review of 54 studies found no strong link between the side-view curves of the spine and back pain. Staying in the same position for a long time, however, can cause stiffness and discomfort; changing position often can help.
kam42: Why does a hunched back increase with age?
kam43: Conditions such as osteoporosis and arthritis, as well as spinal fractures, can increase a hunched back. For bone health, see our osteoporosis guide.
